desc:
Given an integer array nums and an integer target, count the distinct value pairs (a, b) with a ≤ b and a + b = target such that the array contains a and b at two different positions.

Two pairs are the same if they hold the same values, no matter where those values sit in the array. If a = b, the value must therefore occur at least twice.

For example, nums = [1, 1, 2, 45, 46, 46] and target = 47 give 2, namely (1, 46) and (2, 45). For nums = [3, 3, 3] and target = 6 the answer is 1.
hints: Try every pair of positions and put the value pair into a set. That is O(n<sup>2</sup>), which is too slow for 10,000 elements.
For each distinct value x you only need to know whether target - x exists. A hash map of counts answers that in O(1).

Visit every distinct value x. If target - x > x and it exists, count one pair. If target - x == x, count one pair only when x occurs at least twice. Requiring x < target - x avoids counting a pair twice.
editorial: Count the occurrences of every value in a hash map. A distinct pair is identified by its smaller value x and its partner y = target - x. Loop over the distinct values: if x < y, the pair counts when y is present; if x == y, it counts when x appears at least twice. Pairs with x > y were already seen from the other side, so they are skipped.

The loop touches each distinct value once, giving O(n) time and O(n) space. A sorted array with two pointers also works in O(n log n) with O(1) extra space, but you have to skip repeated values carefully to avoid counting the same pair twice.
